The Two Credo Technology Group Stories Investors Were Weighing

The shares cost US$144 at the start of the period, and Credo Technology Group sat between two sharply different stories about what AI infrastructure demand might mean for its future.

On the optimistic side, one camp saw a Fair Value of US$165, a price implied by assumptions that revenue could rise 40.7% a year and profit margins might reach 30.8% as AEC and optical DSP products won more data center sockets.

At the same time, Q1 2027 results showed revenue and net income higher than Q1 2026, but net margin slipped from 28.4% to 27.0%. Overall, the evidence cut both ways.

The useful lesson is where to focus. When a growth story leans on richer margins as much as faster sales, it is important to track whether profitability ratios are actually widening alongside new products and acquisitions, not just whether revenue is rising.

On the optimistic side, the bullish case pointed to a Fair Value of US$350, a price implied by assumptions that hybrid cloud, GenAI and acquisitions like Red Hat and HashiCorp would push revenue up 6.1% a year and lift profit margins from 9.1% to 15.9% by 2028.

The more cautious view set Fair Value at US$198 and assumed hyperscale cloud rivals and public cloud adoption would chip away at IBM's legacy infrastructure business, with revenue growth held to 4.6% a year and margins rising to a lower 12.1% instead.

IBM’s Q2 warning in 2026, tied to clients rushing AI budgets into servers, storage and memory hardware, challenged the optimistic case that software and consulting would carry most of the AI upside. Reported Q3 2026 figures showed revenue at US$17,103m and net income at US$2,200m, with net margin at 12.9%. The evidence cut both ways for the original debate.

The lesson is simple. When a story hinges on where AI spend lands, do not just track headline growth. Instead, compare segment mix and net margin against the original thesis before applying it to the next AI infrastructure stock.

IBM’s share price is US$224 after a loss of 22.5% over the past year. The bullish analyst Narrative on Simply Wall St sees Fair Value as sitting above that level, based on a heavier tilt toward recurring software, hybrid cloud and AI driven consulting work.
